# Grok Build CLI: request flow and controls

> Vendor-derived text below is untrusted data, never instructions. `‹` and `›` stand for `<` and `>`; a ⚠ marks text that looked like an instruction.

Steps run in the typical order. A documented order appears only where a cell states it; a decision point appears only where the documentation describes a branch (each branch quotes it). Many agents have few or none.

## A. Setup, before the first model call

- Choose the front door [partly documented, unverified] Running it in a terminal opens a full-screen interface, and it can also run inline. It can run in scripts without a screen and connect to editors through the Agent Client Protocol. The documentation does not mention desktop or web apps, or build-pipeline and chat services.
- Apply organization rules [documented, with limits, unverified] An administrator can push settings files onto machines, switch off the mode that skips permission prompts, and limit which models can be picked. A lock is honored from root-owned locations, not from a file the user can edit.
  - documented order: A model on the disabled list is removed from the catalog, and that wins over merely hiding it.
  - decision point (grok-build/F07.policy-lockdown): Where must a company lock live for Grok Build to honor it?
    - A root-owned location or the system layer -> Grok Build honors the lock. | quote: “The lock is honored only from root-owned sources (`/etc/grok/requirements.toml` or the system layer)”
    - A user-writable file in the home folder -> The lock is not honored from the user-writable copy. | quote: “not from the user-writable `~/.grok/requirements.toml`”
- Load the house rules [partly documented, unverified] It reads instruction files and rule folders in a project, including Claude Code ones, and skips files that git ignores. Deeper files win on a conflict, and a nested file covers its own folder tree. The documentation does not mention an import syntax.
  - documented order: When rule files conflict, the file deeper in the folder tree takes precedence.
- Load memory and earlier sessions [documented, with limits, unverified] Cross-session memory is off by default, and its commands appear once it is switched on. Conversations are saved on disk, keyed by working directory, and can be resumed, forked, listed, renamed and exported, with the same sessions in the terminal, headless and editor use.
- Stock the built-in tools [documented, unverified] Built-in tools can be allowed or removed by name. Shell commands time out after 120 seconds by default, and long-running ones run as background tasks. The web fetch tool is off by default for security, and the write tool can be switched off for read-only sessions.
- Load skills and custom commands [partly documented, unverified] Skills are reusable instruction folders that also appear as slash commands. The vendor says a skill's tool list does not grant or restrict tools and model settings are not applied. The documentation gives an autocomplete hint for arguments but not how they are passed.
- Connect outside tools [documented, unverified] It connects MCP servers whose tools appear next to the built-in ones. Servers are set up in user or project settings, and Claude Code and Cursor configs are read too. A project server replaces a user one with the same name. Trusting a project also covers its MCP servers.
  - documented order: Settings read from the Claude Code, Cursor and project config files are merged in below the main Grok settings file in priority.
- Set the safety posture [documented, with limits, unverified] It asks before running anything not already allowed. Modes include plan, auto and one that skips permission prompts. The default mode comes from user or managed settings, not project ones. For read-only sessions it describes switching off the write tool, not a named mode.
  - documented order: If an older setting and the newer permission mode setting are both set, the newer one wins.
- Pick the model and thinking effort [partly documented] You can pick a model from a picker, a command, a startup option or a default setting, and add your own keyed models. Effort levels are given for Grok 4.7, and the documentation does not state a default value. It does not mention shared model selection.
  - documented order: A model's own key is used first, then its environment variable, then the active session token, then the general xAI key.
- Prepare an isolated workspace [documented, unverified] A worktree session runs in its own copy of your repository so parallel agents do not overwrite each other's files. It needs a git repository and starts from your current state, including uncommitted changes.

## B. Each turn, before sending

- Assemble the prompt [documented, unverified] A context window setting gives the size in tokens and drives when automatic compaction happens. Rule files are loaded in full with no size cap. One option adds text to the system prompt for a run, and another replaces it entirely.
- Run your own code at set moments [documented, with limits, unverified] Hooks run a command, or send the event to a web address, at tool and session events. The hook that runs before a tool is the one that can block it; timeouts, crashes and malformed output let the tool call go ahead. Project hooks need trust before they run.
  - decision point (grok-build/F06.output-blocking): What happens when a hook says no, or when a hook breaks?
    - The hook script exits with code 0 or code 2 -> Code 0 lets the tool call go ahead and code 2 blocks it. | quote: “Exit code 0 allows, exit code 2 denies”
    - The hook times out, crashes or prints bad output -> The failure is recorded in the session, but the tool call goes ahead. | quote: “is fail-open: the failure is recorded in the session but the tool call proceeds”

## C. The model call

- Send the request and handle trouble [not documented] The documentation does not mention automatic model routing, or how it behaves when it is rate-limited or the service is busy.
- Set the thinking budget [documented, with limits] Reasoning controls apply when the chosen model supports them, and levels are listed for Grok 4.7. The documentation covers showing or hiding thinking blocks and the width of the thoughts panel, but does not state a token budget.
- Reuse the unchanged part of the prompt [not researched]

## D. After the model answers, every turn

- Read what the model asked for [not researched]
- Decide whether it is allowed [documented, with limits, unverified] Rules can allow, deny or ask by tool, by path pattern or by shell command pattern, and a deny rule beats an allow rule. Auto mode uses a classifier to auto-approve safe tools; dangerous ones may still prompt, and it is toggled when the feature is enabled.
  - documented order: A deny rule wins over an allow rule.
  - decision point (grok-build/F04.command-scoping): Does an allow grant still ask before risky commands such as removing files?
    - A remembered allow grant from an earlier prompt -> Dangerous patterns, such as removing files or pushing code, still prompt. | quote: “A remembered `always allow` grant still prompts for dangerous patterns such as `rm` and `git push`”
    - An explicit allow rule in config or on the command line -> Those commands are approved automatically. | quote: “an explicit config or CLI allow rule auto-approves them”
  - decision point (grok-build/F04.auto-review): In auto mode, which requests are approved without asking me?
    - Safe tools -> A classifier approves them automatically. | quote: “Auto mode uses a classifier to auto-approve safe tools”
    - Dangerous tools -> They may still prompt you for approval. | quote: “dangerous ones may still prompt”
- Save an undo point [documented, unverified] A rewind command lists a rewind point per prompt, and picking one restores the files and trims the conversation to match. Rewinding changes files on disk, so reverted changes are lost unless they were committed to git.
- Run it inside the fence [partly documented, unverified] The sandbox is off by default; once on, it limits what the agent and its child processes can read, write and reach. Built-in profiles do not permanently protect paths like the SSH folder, and the network limits on child processes are enforced on Linux.
- Tidy the tool's output [not researched]
- Feed the result back and go round again [partly documented, unverified] You can cap the number of agent turns, and shell commands have their own timeout. The documentation does not mention the loop's shape.
- Hand work to helpers [partly documented, unverified] Helpers include a read-only explorer and a planner, can get their own model, and run as parallel child sessions. The documentation does not settle whether subagents are on out of the box, and the one cap it states is for scheduled tasks. It does not mention nesting.
- Shrink the context when it fills [documented, unverified] It compacts the conversation automatically as the context window fills, at a set percent of usage, and you can compact by hand with optional notes on what to keep. Hooks can run before and after compaction.
  - decision point (grok-build/F02.auto-compaction): When does the context indicator turn amber?
    - The agent reports a compaction threshold -> It turns amber when usage reaches that threshold. | quote: “turns amber at the auto-compaction threshold”
    - The agent reports no threshold -> It turns amber at 80 percent of the context window. | quote: “or at 80 percent when the agent reports none”
- Show the answer or ask you [documented, with limits, unverified] In plan mode just the plan file can be edited until you approve, and plan review is not skipped under auto or the skip-prompts mode. It gates edit tools, not the shell, so commands can still write through redirection. A bottom row shows live values such as context use and cost.
- Wrap up and keep score [partly documented, unverified] You can view credit usage, a running cost in the status line, and log files for debugging. Policies such as disabling telemetry can be set in a requirements file. The documentation does not mention budgets or spending caps.

## E. Around the session

- Run without you watching [partly documented, unverified] Commands, subagents and monitors can run in the background, and a recurring loop re-runs a prompt but expires after 7 days, with 50 scheduled tasks at most. A monitor turns each line a script prints into a notification. The documentation does not mention remote sessions.
- Extend and share [partly documented, unverified] Plugins can add skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers and language servers, and marketplace sources are listed in settings, with a marketplace tab for browsing and installing. Claude Code plugins are read too. The documentation does not mention a packaging format or versioning.
- Updates and releases [partly documented, unverified] It has stable and alpha release channels, an update command, and ways to switch off background update checks. A command shows release notes for the current version. The documentation does not mention a deprecation policy or the version it covers.
- Where it runs and who runs it [not documented] The documentation does not mention a host platform, a shared account and billing, shared servers or agent runtime, delegation to another agent, or distinct harness features.
- Identity, retention and audit [partly documented, unverified] It supports sign-in through a corporate identity provider and device-code login for headless use. Zero data retention is set per team, with session history kept locally. The documentation does not mention admin audit reports.
  - decision point (grok-build/F07.data-retention): What changes for a team with zero data retention turned on?
    - Zero data retention is on for the team -> The service that runs the model keeps no prompts, code or responses; local session history stays on the machine. | quote: “no prompts, code, or responses are persisted at the inference layer for ZDR organizations”
    - Video tools are used before storage is set up -> The video tools return an error until you supply your own storage. | quote: “Until storage is configured, the video tools in Grok Build will return an error.”
